**The Alchemy of Forgotten Things**

I found the journal in the attic last summer—yellowed pages, smelling of mothballs and something older, something *alive*. The handwriting was jagged, as if written in a hurry, but the words clung to the paper like a second skin. The first entry was dated *June 12, 1987*, and it began with a question I’d never asked myself before:

*"What if the things we leave behind aren’t just gone? What if they linger, just out of sight, whispering in the cracks of memory?"*

I didn’t know what to make of it. Maybe it was just a girl’s ramblings, a girl who’d been lost in her own head for too long. Or maybe it was something else entirely—a warning, a secret, a language only the attic could understand.

I started reading it in the dim light of my bedroom, the pages curling slightly as if they’d been kissed by time itself. The entries grew stranger with each turn of the page. There were dates I didn’t recognize—*February 4, 1990*, *October 17, 1992*—and names that didn’t belong to anyone I knew. *"Lena’s voice in the dark,"* it read. *"The way the wind carries her laughter before the storm."*

Then came the drawings. Not sketches, not paintings—*traces*. Faint, as if the artist had used something that had dissolved over time. A half-formed face with too many eyes. A handprint that stretched into a spiderweb. The journal’s owner had been obsessed with the idea of things *existing in the space between being and forgetting*.

One night, I woke to the sound of scratching at my window. Not birds. Not wind. Something *small*, something that moved in slow, deliberate motions. I pulled on my robe and crept outside, the cold air biting my cheeks. There, on the lawn, was a single page from the journal—folded, as if it had been torn from the book itself. The words were scrawled in the same jagged script:

*"You’re not the only one who remembers."*

I turned back inside, but the journal was gone. The attic door was ajar, the light spilling out like a warning. That night, I dreamed of Lena’s voice, of hands reaching from the dark, of things that weren’t supposed to be there.

The next morning, I found the journal back on my nightstand, the pages crisp and whole. But the last entry was new, written in a voice I didn’t recognize:

*"She’s coming. She’s always been coming."*

I didn’t sleep that night. I didn’t sleep for weeks. And then, one evening, I heard it—a whisper in the hallway, just beyond my door. A girl’s voice, soft and familiar.

I opened the door.

She was standing there, her back to me, her hair a wild tangle of dark curls. She wore an old sweater, the sleeves rolled up to her elbows, and her hands were clenched into fists.

*"You found it,"* she said, her voice trembling. *"You found the thing that was supposed to stay hidden."*

I didn’t know what to say. I didn’t know what to do.

She turned around, and for a second, I thought I saw her—Lena, from the journal, from the dreams. But then she was just a girl, no older than me, with eyes that were too bright, too *knowing*.

*"You have to let it go,"* she said. *"The things we leave behind don’t stay gone. They just wait, until the right time."*

I didn’t understand. But I knew, deep down, that she was right.

So I closed the door behind me and walked away. I buried the journal in the garden, where the roots of the old oak tree would swallow it whole. And I never looked back.

But sometimes, when the wind blows just right, I swear I can still hear it—the whispering of things that were never meant to be found.
